Transmute

/trans-MYOOT/ - the stress falls on MYOOT · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Transmute means to change one substance or form into another.

In the cellar's crocks, salt and time transmute shredded cabbage into sauerkraut, a food the raw leaf only hints at.

Worked Example

Her memoir transmutes a bitter childhood into comedy: the cold flat, the absent father, and the terrible school plays return as scenes readers laugh at before they realize what they are laughing at.

Transmute goes beyond mere change: the starting stuff becomes different stuff. Wool dyed blue has been altered; grief worked into a symphony has been transmuted. The word keeps a whiff of alchemy — the old dream of turning one thing into another.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

transform: To transform is to remake something so dramatically that it reads as new — the renovated warehouse, the actor unrecognizable in costume. The change announces itself. Transmute is quieter and deeper at once: it claims the very material has crossed over into a different substance, whatever the surface shows.

recast: To recast is to pour the same material into a new shape or role — a lecture recast as an essay, a myth recast for the stage. The material survives the move; only its form is new. Transmute changes the material itself: lead into gold, grief into music.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

preserve: to keep something exactly as it is

freeze: to hold something unchanged in its current state

Where it sits · how deeply the thing is remade — convert → transmute → transfigure

convert vs. transmute: Convert is milder than transmute — a converted barn is still the same timber put to new use, while transmuted matter has become a different substance altogether.

transfigure vs. transmute: Transfigure goes further than transmute — transmuting changes what a thing is made of, but transfiguring lifts its whole appearance into something radiant and scarcely recognizable.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — trans-

Prefix — trans-: across

Root — mut

Root — mut: to change (Latin mutare)

Put it together

Put it together: Trans- (across) + mut- (to change, Latin mutare) = to change across — from one substance clean over into another. Latin transmutare was the alchemist's verb of choice, and English keeps the full-strength sense: not adjusted, not rearranged, but changed across the line into something else.

Use the root in a new word: mutation

Use the root in a new word: mutation: A single mutation in the gene changes the flower's color from violet to white.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Transmute promises deep change — substance into substance, lead into gold, grief into music. For routine switches, convert is the working word; and where this unit's metamorphosis names the astonishing gap between before and after, transmute points at the material itself crossing over.
